passages.t: A shoot from the stump of Jesse
passages.happening:
‘Then a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse, and a Branch from his roots will bear fruit’ (verse 1).

‘The Spirit of the LORD will rest on Him’ (verse 2), the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and strength, of knowledge and the fear of the LORD. He will delight in the fear of the LORD. He will not judge by what he sees or hears (verse 3), ‘but with righteousness He will judge the poor, and with equity He will decide for the lowly of the earth’ (verse 4). He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth and slay the wicked with the breath of his lips.

‘Righteousness will be the belt around His hips, and faithfulness the sash around His waist’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 10 ended with the LORD felling the forest of Assyria. Chapter 11 turns at once to another stump, the house of Jesse, David's father. The royal line of David, which God had promised to keep on the throne, looked in Isaiah's day like a tree cut to the ground. Kings such as Ahaz had trusted Assyria instead of God, and the prophet had warned that judgment would leave only a remnant. Yet from the stump a shoot will grow.

This chapter gathers up the promises of chapters 7 and 9, the child Immanuel and the son whose government has no end, and describes the king himself. His power is the Spirit of the LORD. His wisdom does not depend on appearances or rumor. His justice is for the poor and the lowly, the very people Judah's rulers had robbed in chapters 1, 3, 5 and 10. His weapon is his word.

The first hearers had watched their kings fail. They were given a picture of the king God would raise up instead.
passages.later: Jeremiah promises the same: ‘I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and He will reign wisely as King and will administer justice and righteousness in the land’ (Jeremiah 23:5). Paul writes of the coming of Christ, ‘whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of His mouth’ (2 Thessalonians 2:8), in words close to verse 4.
passages.asks: This king judges the poor with righteousness and does not decide by what his eyes see. Ask whether you judge people by appearances. And ask what it would mean for the Spirit of counsel and strength to rest on you in your own small sphere.

passages.happening:
‘The wolf will live with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the goat; the calf and young lion and fatling will be together, and a little child will lead them’ (verse 6). The cow will graze with the bear, their young will lie down together, ‘and the lion will eat straw like the ox’ (verse 7). The infant will play by the cobra's den, and the toddler will reach into the viper's nest (verse 8).

‘They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain, for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The king's reign brings a peace so deep that predators and prey lie down together. Every pair is a hunter and its prey: wolf and lamb, leopard and goat, lion and calf, bear and cow, snake and child. And a little child leads them all.

The first hearers knew wolves and lions as real dangers to their flocks and children. This picture says the world the king brings is one where nothing preys on anything, and the most defenseless are safe.

The reason is in verse 9: the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD. Peace flows from knowing God.
passages.later: Isaiah returns to the same picture at the end of the book: ‘The wolf and the lamb will feed together, and the lion will eat straw like the ox’ (Isaiah 65:25). Habakkuk takes up verse 9: ‘the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea’ (Habakkuk 2:14). And Paul speaks of creation itself being ‘set free from its bondage to decay’ (Romans 8:21).
passages.hard:
Will wolves and lions literally stop eating meat, or is this poetry?

Readers take these verses in different ways. Some read them literally, as a description of a renewed creation, in a future earthly reign of Christ or in the new heavens and new earth, where violence among animals truly ends. They note that Genesis 1 gives plants as food and that Romans 8 speaks of creation's release from bondage. Others read the animals as a picture of peoples and nations, with the fierce powers living at peace with the weak, a reading supported by the way Isaiah uses animals for nations elsewhere. Many hold both: the passage is poetry, but the poetry is about a real renewal of the whole world, not only of human hearts.

These notes take no side. What the text plainly teaches on every reading is that the king's reign ends harm and destruction and fills the earth with the knowledge of God.
passages.asks: In this picture a little child leads the animals that once preyed on each other. Ask where in your life something that once threatened you could, by God's grace, lie down in peace. And ask what knowing God has to do with the end of harm.

passages.t: A banner for the nations, and a highway home
passages.happening:
‘On that day the Root of Jesse will stand as a banner for the peoples. The nations will seek Him, and His place of rest will be glorious’ (verse 10).

The Lord will reach out his hand a second time to recover the remnant of his people from Assyria, Egypt, Pathros, Cush, Elam, Shinar, Hamath and the islands of the sea (verse 11). He will raise a banner for the nations and gather the exiles of Israel and the scattered of Judah ‘from the four corners of the earth’ (verse 12). The jealousy of Ephraim will depart, and Judah will no longer harass Ephraim (verse 13). Together they will overcome their old enemies (verse 14).

The LORD will dry up the gulf of the Sea of Egypt and split the Euphrates into seven streams, so people can cross in dry sandals (verse 15). ‘There will be a highway for the remnant of His people who remain from Assyria, as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The list of lands in verse 11 reflects a world of deportation and flight. Assyria and Egypt were the two great powers. Pathros is southern Egypt. Cush is the Nile kingdom south of Egypt. Elam lay east of Babylonia. Shinar is the old name for Babylonia. Hamath was a city on the Orontes River in Syria. The islands of the sea are the Mediterranean shores to the west. Many scholars date parts of verses 10 to 16 later than Isaiah, pointing to the wide scattering they assume; others note that Israelites were already being deported and fleeing in all these directions in the Assyrian age.

The second time God reaches out his hand recalls the first, the exodus from Egypt. The return will be a new exodus, with dry ground through the waters and a highway home.

The old split between the northern and southern kingdoms, Ephraim and Judah, will be healed. Verse 14 pictures the reunited people overcoming the neighbors who had harassed them in Isaiah's day. These are ancient peoples named in the language of their time. The verse is not a key for naming any people of the present day.
passages.later: Paul quotes verse 10 as he speaks of the Gentiles: ‘The Root of Jesse will appear, One who will arise to rule over the Gentiles; in Him the Gentiles will put their hope’ (Romans 15:12). And the highway of verse 16 returns in Isaiah's later chapters: ‘make a straight highway for our God in the desert’ (Isaiah 40:3).
passages.asks: God promises to heal the old rivalry between Ephraim and Judah. Ask what old rivalry in your family, church or community needs God's healing. And ask what it means that the king of this chapter is a banner the nations will seek, not only his own people.
